method.purpose: Human-authored qualitative study of how released songs connect narrative meaning to musical treatment.
method.boundary: Only factual metadata, paraphrased narrative summaries, broad arrangement observations, and generalized design lessons are recorded. No lyric text, audio, score, chord transcription, or reusable note sequence is stored.

cases.lesson: Joy does not require major mode. Fast pulse, short articulation, groove, claps, and communal voices can dominate the emotional reading.

cases.narrativeSummary: A private confrontation with a former partner moving on.
cases.lesson: A major key can carry grief when tempo is slow, accompaniment is exposed, repetition feels inescapable, and the performance arc does the emotional work.

cases.narrativeSummary: Relief after a long period of pressure, expressed through the return of spring.
cases.lesson: Hope feels earned when motion and color accumulate gradually. A rising story benefits from a restrained opening, increasing rhythmic life, and a brighter counterline near the release.

cases.narrativeSummary: Exhaustion, entrapment, and dissatisfaction are presented through a deliberately comforting surface.
cases.lesson: Narrative and surface emotion can oppose each other. The contrast works only when the gentle texture remains fragile and unresolved rather than simply cheerful.

cases.narrativeSummary: Public isolation and rejection inside a crowded club.
cases.lesson: Sadness can retain physical momentum. For high-arousal mixed emotion, keep the pulse but preserve tension, reduce harmonic closure, and create one exposed pause before returning.

cases.narrativeSummary: A working-class escape attempt gradually reveals another cycle of confinement.
cases.lesson: A story can begin with hope without earning a triumphant ending. Repetition, restrained growth, and reduced final closure are useful for narratives that circle back instead of resolving.

cases.narrativeSummary: Displacement, regret, and a wish to escape the consequences of a broken relationship.

musicalTreatment.mode: C major frequently falling into A minor
texture: familiar seasonal contour reharmonized toward minor

cases.lesson: Contextual memory can deepen grief when familiar color is harmonically displaced. The product should use this as an abstract contrast principle, never copy a recognizable borrowed melody.

cases.narrativeSummary: Difficult times end and pent-up energy is released.
cases.lesson: Release can be communicated by adding human, imperfect layers and widening the ensemble toward the climax instead of relying on a synthetic riser or a sudden octave jump.

cases.artist: Tears for Fears; Michael Andrews and Gary Jules
cases.lesson: The same narrative can feel restless or devastated depending on instrumentation and density. Arrangement selection is part of semantic interpretation, not decoration after composition.

cases.narrativeSummary: A deliberate affirmation of shared beauty written against social turmoil.
cases.lesson: Hope can gain weight from restraint. A positive story does not always need speed; warmth, spacious timing, and an assured ending can communicate mature optimism.

distilledPrinciples.rule: Treat mode as one signal among tempo, articulation, groove, register, timbre, and closure. Never infer the whole emotion from major or minor alone.
Choose density and instruments from narrative meaning before adding decorative layers. Sparse acoustic treatment and forceful rhythmic treatment can tell different truths about the same story.
When positive and negative dimensions are both strong, preserve some brightness or pulse while increasing tension and reducing closure instead of averaging everything into mild sadness.
For rising stories, build rhythmic activity, counterline, dynamics, and ensemble width gradually; do not fake a climax with an isolated octave jump.
For falling or cyclical stories, let the outro lose energy or closure even if the opening contains hope.
Low-arousal confession benefits from fewer attacks, longer sustain, narrower range, and exposed acoustic timbre.
